newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Forecast-WoodCommerz sees Czech 1997 GDP +2.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: Forecast-WoodCommerz sees Czech 1997 GDP +2.0 pct.

text.p: Prague-based investment house WoodCommerz said on Thursday it had lowered its full-year 1997 Czech gross domestic product growth forecast to 2.0 percent from 4.0 percent as deep economic imbalances bite.

Presenting his report to journalists, chief economist Jiri Krovak also said he expected the Czech crown to fall further to 34-35 to the dollar by the year's end after sharp pressure in May forced the central bank to float the currency.

He said profound deficiencies in industrial restructuring were inhibiting growth and led to real GDP rising a paltry 1.5 percent in the first quarter after 4.4 percent growth for the whole of 1996 and 4.8 percent in the first quarter last year.

"The basic cause for the slowing of growth is on the supply side and the lower structural adaptability of the economy which is brought about by the insufficient restructualisation on the micro level," Krovak said, adding that acceleration of bankruptcies and capital market reforms were necessary.
He said that most troubling in the first quarter results released by the Czech Statistical Bureau on Thursday was the 43.7 percent jump, year-on-year, in real inventories.

Factoring out the 22.7 billion crowns in 1997 first quarter adjusted inventories compared with the 15.8 billion crowns in 1996, the quarterly year-on-year real GDP change would be a more than one percent contraction, not 1.5 percent growth.

Despite a more than 10 percent drop in the crown in late May, WoodCommerz forecast the current account deficit to grow to 11.1 percent of gross domestic product by the year's end, compared with just over eight percent in 1996.

The 1997 current account deficit outlook was an improvement from the WoodCommerz forecast in March of 11.5 percent percent of GDP, but assumed the crown falling to 34 to 35 crowns to the dollar by the year's end from current levels of just above 32.

Krovak said that the unpopular centre-right government would have a tough time negotitating and approving its two austerity packages of budget cuts and wage freezes announced in April and May which are aimed at slowing domestic demand.

The latest WoodCommerz report forecasts inflation to rise to 9.5 percent year-on-year by December from May's latest result of 6.3 percent, saying the weakening of the crown adds another 1.5 percent points to the inflation outlook.
